newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr higher at Tokyo noon, recovers to 1.7 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr higher at Tokyo noon, recovers to 1.7 marks.

text.p: The dollar firmed against the yen by midday Tokyo on Tuesday on buying by investors, while it clawed back to 1.700 marks on short-covering by U.S. funds after finding brisk bids at around 1.6950-60 marks.
Dealers said they expect the dollar/yen to stay range-bound before the Group of Seven (G7) meeting on Sunday but to resume rising if there are no surprises at the meeting.
Dealers said remarks by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka gave traders the impression that the G7 meeting would just reconfirm an agreement in February and nothing new may emerge.

Asked whether the G7 would confirm an agreement on currencies reached at its last meeting in Berlin in February, Mitsuzuka told reporters: "Yes, we will reaffirm the basics of the Berlin G7 agreement".
"There is a feeling that the upcoming G7 meeting may not yield anything special, which made the dollar's downside well-bid by luring purchases from Japanese investors," said a city bank dealer.

Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday that Japan's monetary policy aims to ensure a basis for economic recovery while keeping watch over economic conditions. This implied that the BOJ would stick to the current rock-bottom interest rates for a while.

A medium-sized Japanese life insurer was said to have bought dollars at around 125.30 yen but sold some of them above 125.50 yen. Some dealers noted that the life insurer apparently got involved in currency dealings. Bids by U.S. funds at around 125.30 yen also induced short-covering by dealers and sent it as high as 125.73 yen by midday Tokyo.

Light stop-loss dollar buying is expected at 125.80-90 yen, but fears of BOJ dollar-selling intervention above 126 yen would probably cap the dollar's advance, said a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo.

Views were mixed among dealers over the direction of dollar/mark in the near term. Political uncertainty ahead of elections in some countries in Europe, such as France and Britain, have encouraged operators to shift to marks as a safe-haven currency. This strengthened the mark against the dollar overnight. But some dealers said mark buying for the dollar mostly complete due to morning's short-covering.
"I don't think that dollar/mark has moved out of the 1.7000 to 1.7500 mark range," said a U.S. bank dealer. "There were relatively solid bids around 1.6960 marks."
A Japanese bank dealer said there was a chance of the dollar falling a further one to two pfennigs against the mark, but he thought the dollar's downside correction was ending.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday that a delay in EMU was possible if "big countries" fail to meet the entry requirements. This briefly sparked demand for mark buying overnight, dealers said.
